Hook: In 2010 two of the most respected economists in the world, Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff, published a short paper called Growth in a Time of Debt. They sorted twenty advanced economies' years since 1946 by the size of the government's debt. Below thirty percent of GDP, growth averaged 4.1 percent a year; between thirty and ninety, about three. Above ninety percent, the average they reported was minus 0.1 percent. Growth seemed simply to stop once debt passed ninety percent of GDP, and the threshold was quoted in debates over austerity on both sides of the Atlantic.

Three years later a graduate student at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, Thomas Herndon, was asked to replicate a well-known result for a class, and chose this one. He could not. Reinhart and Rogoff kindly sent him their spreadsheet. The formula that averaged the countries ran over rows thirty to forty-four, not thirty to forty-nine. Five countries had been left out: Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada and Denmark. With his professors Michael Ash and Robert Pollin he found two further choices that mattered even more: some years of high debt and decent growth were left out, and each country's average counted the same, whether it spent one year above ninety percent or nineteen. Corrected, growth above ninety percent averaged 2.2 percent, lower than below it, but nothing like a cliff. This part takes the government's budget seriously, and the evidence about it more seriously still.

This part's question: what can a government's budget do for the economy, and how much debt is too much? When does debt grow, and what does it take to hold it steady? How much does a dollar of government spending or taxes move output, and how can anyone tell? And when do debts become dangerous, and why do countries repay them at all?
Economics, Built. Part thirty-two: the treasury.

Here is the plan. The government's budget constraint and how debt evolves, which turns on the gap between the interest rate and growth; then you balance a budget. The multiplier in theory, and in four kinds of evidence, and what tax changes do. Automatic stabilizers, the fight over austerity, and the ninety percent threshold recomputed from the original data. Whether debt is a burden at all, why debt should absorb wars, and a theory in which the budget sets the price level. Sovereign default as a model solved on screen, modern monetary theory, and two dials.
Budget: Chapter one. The budget constraint and r minus g.

Start with the budget constraint. Next year the government owes this year's debt plus interest, less whatever it collects beyond its spending on everything but interest: its primary surplus. What matters is debt relative to the economy that carries it, so divide by output. Debt to GDP is multiplied each year by one plus the interest rate over one plus the growth rate, and reduced by the primary surplus as a share of GDP. So when the interest rate r exceeds the growth rate g, debt grows by itself; when r is below g, it shrinks by itself, even with a small deficit. The surplus that holds debt steady is r minus g, over one plus g, times the debt. Evsey Domar made this point in 1944.

Here it is on the Island. Debt equal to a year's output, a primary deficit of two percent of output, and growth of two percent. If the interest rate is two points above growth, debt reaches 337 percent of GDP in forty years, and keeps going. If the two are equal, 180 percent: the deficits simply pile up. If the rate is two points below growth, debt settles near 101 percent, despite the deficit every year. Dashed, the same three economies with a balanced primary budget: with r above g, even that is not enough. Everything about debt sustainability is in the sign of r minus g.

America's own record. Federal debt held by the public was a few percent of GDP before the First World War and 33 percent after it. The Second World War took it to about 115 percent. By 1974 it was 23 percent, mostly not because the war debt was repaid: it fell as a share of a growing economy, with interest rates held below growth and inflation, which is r below g. Since 2007 it has risen again, to 97 percent of GDP now.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: the minister's budget.

Your turn. You are the Island's finance minister. The government owes a full year of the Island's output. It pays 3 percent interest, and the economy grows 2 percent a year. This year, spending other than interest exceeds taxes by 2 percent of GDP. You want to stop the debt ratio from rising, and no more than that.
What primary balance holds the debt at a hundred percent of GDP? A surplus of about one percent of GDP; a balanced primary budget; or is a deficit of one percent enough? Pause, and choose.

Interest is a point above growth, so with debt equal to output the government needs a primary surplus of 0.98 percent of GDP: answer A. From a deficit of two percent, that is a swing of 3.0 percent of GDP in spending cuts or tax rises. If each dollar of austerity costs half a dollar of output, output falls about 1.5 percent; if it costs one and a half, about 4.5. And a smaller economy makes the same debt a larger share of it, so with a large multiplier, austerity can raise the debt ratio before it lowers it. Everything turns on the size of the multiplier, which is what the rest of this part is about.
Theory: Chapter three. The multiplier in theory.

Theory gives three answers. The Keynesian cross of Part 27: a dollar the government spends is someone's income, part of which is spent again, and again. With sixty cents of each extra dollar spent, the multiplier is two and a half. But spending can raise interest rates, which cut private investment: crowding out. And households who expect the taxes that will pay for the spending may spend less themselves, as Robert Barro argued. In the New Keynesian model of Part 30, the answer depends above all on the central bank.

Here is the multiplier in Part 30's model, for spending that fades at different speeds. With a central bank that follows Taylor's rule, extra spending raises inflation and the bank raises its rate, crowding out private demand. The multiplier is below one: 0.75 for spending that halves each quarter, and smaller the longer it lasts. Now put the economy at the zero bound, with the rate stuck at zero for as long as the spending lasts. Extra spending raises expected inflation, which lowers the real interest rate instead of raising it: the multiplier is 1.13, and 2.7 if the trap and the spending are more persistent. Michael Woodford, and Lawrence Christiano, Martin Eichenbaum and Sergio Rebelo, showed this in 2011. Past the dashed line, the model has no stable answer at all. Theory says the multiplier is not one number. It depends on the state of the economy and on the central bank.
Evidence: Chapter four. The multiplier in evidence.

Measuring the multiplier runs into Part 31's problem: governments spend more in recessions, so spending and output move together for reasons that are not the multiplier. Four designs get around it. Timing: budgets are set months in advance, so the part of this quarter's spending that surprises is a shock; Olivier Blanchard and Roberto Perotti used it in 2002. Military news: Valerie Ramey read the press for news of wars and buildups and valued it in dollars, because markets and households react to news, not to the delivery of tanks. Regions: Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson compared states that get more defence contracts when national defence spending rises. And forecast errors: where austerity was planned, did growth fall short of the forecasts?

Here are the first two designs on the longest record there is: American data since 1889, assembled by Valerie Ramey and Sarah Zubairy, with the World Wars and Korea in it. For each horizon, output and spending are projected on the shock, and the multiplier is the extra output so far over the extra spending so far. With military news, in red: 0.67 after two years, 0.71 after four. With Blanchard and Perotti's timing, in teal: 0.41. Both are below one. When the federal government spent more, private spending fell, on average over a century. These are this film's estimates from their data; they match the published ones to two decimal places.

Theory said the multiplier should be larger in slumps and at the zero bound. Split the century by unemployment: in normal times, 0.59 after two years; with unemployment above six and a half percent, 0.62. In quarters with interest rates near zero, 0.74. Ramey and Zubairy found no sign that slack makes the multiplier large. Studies using other methods, notably Alan Auerbach and Yuriy Gorodnichenko's, found much larger multipliers in recessions, and the difference between them is still argued.

The third design compares regions. On the Island we can see what it measures. 48 regions share one central bank for 40 years. National spending lands more in some than in others. Compare regions within the same year, and output rises 1.46 for each point of extra spending, close to the planted local multiplier of one and a half. But the nation as a whole gains only 0.64, because the central bank leans against national spending, and the region-by-region comparison cannot see that: it is absorbed in what all regions share in a year, the missing intercept. Nakamura and Steinsson found a regional multiplier of about one and a half in American states; Gabriel Chodorow-Reich's survey of such studies, about one point eight. Both are honest answers to a different question from the national one.
Taxes: Chapter five. Tax changes: the narrative record.

Taxes have the same problem: governments cut taxes in recessions. Christina and David Romer read the record behind every postwar American tax law, the speeches, the committee reports, the president's messages, to learn why each was passed. They kept the changes made for long-run reasons, to promote growth or because of a view about the size of government, or to pay off a deficit already there. They dropped changes made because the economy was weak or strong, or to pay for a war. What is left, in percent of GDP: gold for increases, green for cuts.

What followed? Project real GDP on the exogenous changes, quarter by quarter after a tax increase of one percent of GDP. Output falls slowly, and by 2.2 percent after 10 quarters on this film's estimate. The Romers' own estimate was a fall of nearly three percent over three years. A tax multiplier of two to three is larger than most estimates for spending, which is the opposite of what the simple Keynesian cross predicts. Part of the answer may be that taxes change incentives to work and invest, and much of the effect in their data came through investment; why the gap is so large is still argued.
Stabilizers: Much of fiscal policy needs no decision at all. Here is the federal budget balance since 1948, as a share of GDP, and unemployment. They are close to mirror images. On average, each point of extra unemployment has come with a budget balance about 1.2 points worse in the same year. In 2009 the deficit reached 9.8 percent of GDP, in 2020 14.7. Part of each was decided: stimulus laws. Part happened automatically: income and profit taxes fall when incomes fall, and unemployment benefits rise. Those automatic stabilizers cushion spending without waiting for Congress.

And then there are the cheques, from Part 22. In 2001 and in 2008, households spent a sizeable share of their rebates within months of receiving them. The dates of the payments were set by the last digits of social security numbers, effectively at random, so households who were paid early can be compared with those paid later. A cheque in a slump stimulates spending, which is evidence against the full Ricardian equivalence the next chapters examine.
Austerity: Chapter seven. Austerity, and the ninety percent threshold recomputed.

After 2010 governments in Europe argued that cutting deficits could raise growth by restoring confidence. Alberto Alesina and Silvia Ardagna had found that large consolidations, especially those made by cutting spending, sometimes came with growth. The reply was the identification problem again. A deficit that shrinks in the data often shrinks because good times are already coming, which flatters austerity. Jaime Guajardo, Daniel Leigh and Andrea Pescatori did what the Romers did for taxes: they found consolidations in policy documents, adopted to cut deficits rather than in response to the economy, and those lowered output. Ask why the budget changed, and austerity looks contractionary, as the evidence on multipliers says it should.

Now the ninety percent result, recomputed here from Herndon, Ash and Pollin's copy of the original data. The published figure: minus 0.1 percent. Use New Zealand's growth as it is in the data, rather than the figure transcribed: minus 0.0. Put the five countries back: 0.3. Put back the years of high debt and decent growth in Australia, Canada and New Zealand that had been left out: 1.9. And count each country-year once, rather than giving New Zealand's single year the weight of Britain's nineteen: 2.2 percent. Growth above ninety percent is slower than in the bands below it, 3.2 percent between sixty and ninety, but there is no cliff.

Here is every country-year in the data. There is a mild downward drift, but nothing happens at ninety percent. And the correlation does not say which way the arrow points: a recession or a decade of slow growth raises the ratio of debt to GDP by itself, through the denominator and through the deficits slumps bring. Reinhart and Rogoff acknowledged the spreadsheet error and defended the broader point that high debt goes with slower growth. That correlation survives. The threshold, and the direction of cause, do not follow from it.
Burden: Chapter eight. Is debt a burden?

Is government debt a burden on the future? Three views. Robert Barro argued in 1974 that debt is only taxes delayed. Households who care about their heirs save to pay them, and nothing real changes: Ricardian equivalence. Peter Diamond's economy of overlapping generations, from Part 23, says the opposite: debt soaks up savings that would otherwise have built capital, so future workers have less to work with. The evidence of Part 22, households spending cheques at once, says equivalence fails in practice. And in 2019 Olivier Blanchard, in his presidential address to the American Economic Association, pointed out that when the safe interest rate is below the growth rate, debt can be rolled over and shrink as a share of output by itself, so its cost may be smaller than it looks.

Here is r minus g for the United States since 1954. The interest rate on one-year Treasury bills, and on ten-year bonds, dashed, less the growth of nominal GDP. The one-year rate was below growth in 76 percent of years, the ten-year in 61 percent. The big exceptions were the 1980s, when Volcker's rates were far above growth, and slumps such as 2009 and 2020, when growth itself collapsed. Blanchard's point: in American history r below g has been the rule. That does not make debt free. Rates can rise, as they did after 2022, and debt still competes with capital for savings. But it changes the arithmetic of how much is too much.
Smoothing: Chapter nine. Tax smoothing: why debt should absorb wars.

How should a government pay for a war? Robert Barro's answer, in 1979, starts from one fact of public finance: the harm a tax does, by discouraging work and saving, rises with the square of its rate. So suppose spending jumps from twenty to fifty percent of output for five years. Raising taxes to fifty percent for those years would be very costly. Better to set a tax rate of 24.0 percent, now and for ever, and let debt absorb the war and be paid down slowly afterwards. Paying as you go would cost the Island 18 percent more in lost output from taxes. Debt is a shock absorber.

That is roughly how wars have been paid for. American debt rose in both World Wars, from 40 percent of GDP in 1941 to 109 in 1946, and then fell for decades as the economy outgrew it, to 44 percent by 1960. Britain financed its wars against Napoleon the same way. Smoothing does not mean debt never matters; it means the time to reduce it is in peacetime and in good years.
FTPL: Chapter ten. Who backs the money? The fiscal theory.

Now a theory in which the budget sets the price level. Government bonds promise money, not goods. Their real value, nominal debt over the price level, must equal what the government will raise to pay them: the present value of its future surpluses. Nominal debt of 100, a real surplus of 2 a year, a real interest rate of 2 percent: the price level is 1. If people come to expect surpluses of only 1.5, the same debt is worth less in goods, and with the debt fixed in money, prices must rise 33 percent. That is the fiscal theory of the price level, from Christopher Sims, Michael Woodford and John Cochrane: if surpluses do not adjust to the debt, the price level does. A central bank controls inflation only as long as the treasury stands behind its debts.

An older warning makes the same point. In 1981 Thomas Sargent and Neil Wallace imagined a treasury that runs a deficit it will not change, and a central bank that must decide how much of it to pay for by printing money. If the bank pays its share from the start, money grows at a steady rate, in teal. If it holds money tight for 12 years, the treasury borrows more instead, and debt piles up. When the bank can no longer refuse, it must pay for the larger debt's interest as well: money growth for ever after is 12.6 percent instead of 11.0. Tight money today means more inflation tomorrow, unless the treasury changes course.
Default: Why do countries repay at all? No court can seize a sovereign's assets at home. Jonathan Eaton and Mark Gersovitz's answer, in 1981, was reputation: a country that defaults is shut out of borrowing for a while, and loses the ability to smooth its spending through bad years. Defaults are also costly at home: output falls, and banks holding the bonds are hit. So a country repays as long as the cost of defaulting exceeds what it would save. Cristina Arellano turned this into a model that can be solved and simulated, calibrated to Argentina. Here it is, solved on this computer by iterating the value functions until they stop changing.

Two things come out of it. First, the price lenders pay for the country's bonds. With little debt, a bond paying one next quarter sells for nearly one. As the country borrows more, the chance of default rises and the price falls, and it falls sooner in a bad quarter, in red, than in a good one, in green: the country can borrow least when it needs to most. Second, the debt a country will still repay rises with its output. Below the line it repays; above it, it defaults. So defaults happen in recessions, as in the data.

Now let the model run for a hundred years. Output wanders. The red lines are defaults, and the shading the years the country is shut out of markets, which ends at random. Each default follows a fall in output. Over a long simulation, defaults come at 2.9 percent a year, close to the three percent Arellano matched for Argentina, and lenders charge 4.4 points over the safe rate on average to cover the risk.

Real defaults look like this. Greece's ten-year yield against Germany's. By early 2012 Greece was paying 29 percent, which no country could pay for long. In March 2012 private holders of Greek bonds exchanged them for new ones with 53.5 percent less face value: the biggest sovereign debt restructuring in history. Argentina had defaulted at the end of 2001, after three years of recession, just as the model predicts. Inside a currency union, as Part 31 showed, a country cannot inflate its debts away, and default is the remaining exit.
Practice: Chapter fourteen. In practice: budget offices and debt managers.

Who does this for a living? Budget offices, such as America's Congressional Budget Office, estimate what every bill costs and how it moves the economy; Part 58 takes one apart. Debt managers in finance ministries decide how much to borrow, at what maturities and in which instruments, which matters more when rates rise. Economists at finance ministries and the IMF forecast with the budget built in, and judge whether debts are sustainable. Their tools are this part's: the budget constraint, r minus g, and multipliers, with honest bands around each.

Called it? In April 2010 the IMF forecast growth for 2010 and 2011 in each European economy, knowing each government's plans to cut its deficit. If the forecasters had used the right multiplier, the errors should have had nothing to do with the size of the plans. Here are the errors against the planned consolidation, recomputed from Olivier Blanchard and Daniel Leigh's data. The slope is -1.10: each extra point of GDP of austerity came with growth about one point below forecast. Greece, on the right, missed by the most. The forecasts had underestimated the multiplier by about one. Wrong, and the IMF's own chief economist said so.
Frontier: Chapter fifteen. Frontier: fiscal space when r is near g.

The frontier is a world in which r is no longer far below g. Federal interest payments reached 5.0 percent of GDP in the 1980s and 1990s, when rates were high. In the 2010s they fell to as little as 1.8 percent, although debt was rising, because rates were so low. Now they are 4.0 percent of GDP, about 1.3 trillion dollars a year, with debt at 97 percent of GDP. Blanchard's arithmetic still holds, but the margin is thinner: the same debt costs more as r rises toward g.

The open questions. How far debt can rise before interest rates rise with it. Whether multipliers really are larger in slumps and at the zero bound. How to pay for the investment the climate transition needs: by borrowing, by taxes, or by pricing carbon, which Part 48 takes up. How fiscal and monetary policy share the job of controlling inflation. And why tax multipliers look so much larger than spending ones.
